title: The Lottery That Lost Money to a Shopkeeper

beats.text: They say the lottery is a tax on people who can't do maths.
In two thousand three, a retired shopkeeper in a small Michigan town did the maths. And he found a lottery that was losing money to him.
Over the next nine years, he and his wife won almost twenty-seven million dollars in prizes. Legally.
This is the story of Jerry and Marge Selbee.
Evart, Michigan. A small town, a long way from anywhere.
For seventeen years, Jerry and Marge ran the convenience store there. Milk, bread, coffee, and lottery tickets.
Jerry had studied mathematics at college. He liked puzzles. Patterns. Numbers that didn't quite add up.
In two thousand three, already retired, he picked up a brochure for a new lottery game called Winfall.
Most lotteries work the same way. If nobody wins the jackpot, it grows. And grows.
Winfall had a twist. If the jackpot passed five million dollars and nobody matched all six numbers, it didn't keep growing. It rolled down.
All that money was shared out among the smaller prizes. The people who matched five numbers, or four, or three.
Jerry read the rules and, by one account, saw the flaw in less than two minutes.
On a roll-down week, the small prizes grew so big that, on average, a ticket was worth more than the dollar it cost.
Buy enough tickets, and the maths was on your side.
Think of it like this. Normally, a lottery pays out less in prizes than it takes in. That gap is the lottery's profit, and it's why players lose over time.
Imagine a raffle with a hundred tickets at a dollar each, and a prize of fifty dollars. Buy every ticket, and you spend a hundred dollars to win fifty.
Now imagine one week where the prize suddenly jumps to a hundred and fifty. Buy every ticket, and you spend a hundred to win a hundred and fifty.
That was a roll-down week. The trick was buying so many tickets that luck evened out, and the averages took over.
Jerry didn't tell Marge at first. He drove to a store in the next town, and bought two thousand two hundred dollars' worth of tickets.
He checked them by hand at the kitchen table. They'd won two thousand one hundred and fifty. A small loss.
He hadn't bought enough to beat the luck. So next time, he bought more. And then more again.
He bet eight thousand dollars, and won fifteen thousand seven hundred.
Then he told Marge.
Marge didn't tell him to stop. She was good at keeping track of things.
They set up a company, G. S. Investment Strategies, and sold shares at five hundred dollars each. First to their children. Then to friends in Evart.
On roll-down weeks, they bought tickets by the thousand. Then every one of them had to be checked, by hand, for hours on end.
In May two thousand five, Michigan shut Winfall down, with no warning.
But Jerry had heard of a similar game in Massachusetts, called Cash WinFall. It rolled down even sooner, at two million dollars.
So whenever a roll-down was coming, Jerry and Marge drove from Michigan to Massachusetts. Hundreds of miles. Then they bought more tickets.
They weren't the only ones who had noticed.
A group of students from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology had spotted the same flaw. Led by a student called James Harvey, they formed their own group, called Random Strategies.
In one roll-down, the M. I. T. group reportedly bet seventeen million dollars in just seven hours.
In twenty eleven, journalists noticed that a handful of groups were winning a huge share of the prizes.
The state's inspector general investigated. The Selbees were never charged with anything. They had simply played by the rules.
Cash WinFall ended in January twenty twelve.
Over nine years, the Selbees' group won almost twenty-seven million dollars in prizes.
After paying for all those tickets, the profit was about seven point seven five million dollars, shared among everyone who'd bought in.
Jerry and Marge stayed in Evart. In twenty twenty-two, their story became a Hollywood film, Jerry and Marge Go Large.
They didn't beat the lottery. They read the rules more carefully than the people who wrote them.
Most weeks, the lottery still wins. But for a few days at a time, the lottery was beating itself. And a retired shopkeeper with a pencil noticed first.
